questions.prompt: A critical bugfix was committed on the release branch. You need to apply only that specific commit to your development branch without merging the entire release branch. Which command should you use?

options.text: git merge --single
git apply
git cherry-pick
git rebase --onto dev release

questions.explanation: git cherry-pick applies the changes from a specific commit onto your current branch as a new commit. Unlike merge, it doesn't bring in any other commits from the source branch — only the one you specify.

questions.prompt: Which statement about Java Records (Java 16+) is true? ```java record Point(int x, int y) {} ```

options.text: Records can be extended by other records to add more fields
Record fields are mutable by default and can be changed after creation

Records are implicitly final with auto-generated equals(), hashCode(), and accessor methods

questions.explanation: Records are implicitly final and cannot be extended. They auto-generate a canonical constructor, accessor methods (x(), y()), equals(), hashCode(), and toString(). The fields (components) are final and private. Records can implement interfaces but cannot extend other classes.

questions.prompt: When does a greedy algorithm guarantee an optimal solution?

options.text: Whenever the problem can be divided into subproblems
When the problem has both the greedy choice property and optimal substructure
When the input is sorted beforehand
When the problem has overlapping subproblems

questions.explanation: A greedy algorithm guarantees optimality only when the problem has the greedy choice property (a locally optimal choice leads to a globally optimal solution) AND optimal substructure. Many problems have optimal substructure but lack the greedy choice property, requiring DP instead.

questions.prompt: Consider the following sorting algorithms: bubble sort, merge sort, quicksort, and selection sort. Which of them are stable by default (equal elements maintain their relative order)?

options.text: Merge sort and quicksort
Bubble sort and selection sort
Bubble sort and merge sort
All four are stable

questions.explanation: A stable sort preserves the relative order of equal elements. Bubble sort and merge sort are stable by default. Selection sort is unstable because it swaps non-adjacent elements. Quicksort is typically unstable due to its partitioning scheme.

questions.prompt: Huffman coding is a greedy algorithm for data compression. Given character frequencies A:45, B:13, C:12, D:16, E:9, F:5, which two characters are combined first in building the Huffman tree?

options.text: A and B (highest frequencies should merge first)
C and D (middle frequencies balance the tree)
E and F (the two lowest frequencies are merged first)
B and C (closest frequencies should merge first)

questions.explanation: Huffman's algorithm always combines the two nodes with the lowest frequencies. Here, the lowest are F (5) and E (9), which are merged into a node with frequency 14. This greedy strategy ensures that less frequent characters get longer codes, minimizing the total encoded length.

questions.prompt: What is the primary risk of this code in a multithreaded environment? ```java class SharedCounter { private int count = 0; public void increment() { count++; } public int getCount() { return count; } } ```

options.text: Deadlock between increment() and getCount()
Race condition — count++ is not atomic and updates can be lost
Stack overflow from recursive calls
Memory leak because count is a primitive

questions.explanation: The `count++` operation is not atomic — it involves read, increment, and write. Without synchronization, two threads can read the same value simultaneously, both increment it, and write back the same result, losing one update. This is a classic race condition. Deadlock and stack overflow are unrelated issues here.

questions.prompt: During a DFS traversal of a directed graph, you encounter an edge (u, v) where v is currently on the recursion stack (in the GRAY/visiting state). What does this indicate?

options.text: The graph has a topological ordering that includes this edge
The graph contains a cycle involving this edge
Node v is a tree edge in the DFS forest
The graph is bipartite

questions.explanation: In DFS coloring, a node on the recursion stack is in the GRAY state (started but not finished). An edge to a GRAY node forms a back edge, which proves the existence of a cycle. This is the standard technique for cycle detection in directed graphs.

questions.prompt: An algorithm sorts an array in O(n log n) worst-case time and uses O(n) extra space. It is also stable. Which algorithm does this describe?

options.text: Quicksort
Heap sort
Insertion sort
Merge sort

questions.explanation: Merge sort guarantees O(n log n) worst-case time and is stable, but requires O(n) extra space for merging. Quicksort averages O(n log n) but has O(n²) worst case. Heap sort is O(n log n) worst case with O(1) space but is not stable.

questions.prompt: How can you find the number of connected components in an undirected graph with V vertices and E edges?

options.text: Count the number of vertices with degree zero
Run Dijkstra's from every vertex and check distances
Count how many times you start a new BFS/DFS from an unvisited vertex
Subtract the number of edges from the number of vertices

questions.explanation: Starting a BFS or DFS from an unvisited vertex explores its entire connected component. Counting how many times you need to start a new traversal gives the number of connected components. Union-Find also works but BFS/DFS is the most straightforward approach.

questions.prompt: How does Go determine if a struct implements an interface? ```go type Stringer interface { String() string } type Dog struct{ Name string } func (d Dog) String() string { return d.Name } ```

options.text: Implicitly — if Dog has all methods defined by Stringer, it satisfies the interface
Dog must be registered with the Stringer interface at runtime
Interfaces in Go cannot be implemented by structs, only by other interfaces
Dog must include 'implements Stringer' in its declaration

questions.explanation: Go uses implicit interface implementation — there is no `implements` keyword. If a type has all the methods that an interface requires, it automatically satisfies that interface. Dog has a String() method matching the Stringer interface, so Dog implements Stringer without any explicit declaration.

questions.prompt: Dijkstra's algorithm fails to find correct shortest paths when the graph contains negative-weight edges. Consider a graph with nodes A→B (weight 5), A→C (weight 2), C→B (weight −4). What shortest distance to B does Dijkstra report versus the actual shortest?

options.text: Dijkstra reports 5, actual is −2
Dijkstra reports −2, actual is −2
Dijkstra reports 2, actual is −2
Dijkstra detects the negative edge and throws an error

questions.explanation: Dijkstra processes B at distance 5 via the direct A→B edge and marks it as finalized. It never reconsiders B after discovering the cheaper path A→C→B (cost 2 + (−4) = −2). The greedy assumption that finalized distances are optimal breaks with negative edges.

questions.prompt: What happens when you add a duplicate element to a `HashSet` in Java? ```java Set set = new HashSet(); set.add("apple"); boolean result = set.add("apple"); System.out.println(result + " " + set.size()); ```

options.text: false 1 — the duplicate is silently ignored and add() returns false
An IllegalArgumentException is thrown
true 2 — duplicates are allowed in sets
false 2 — it returns false but still adds the element

questions.explanation: HashSet does not allow duplicates. When you try to add an element that already exists, the `add()` method returns false and the set remains unchanged. The size stays 1.

questions.prompt: Which access modifier allows a field to be accessed by subclasses in a different package but NOT by unrelated classes in that package?

options.text: private
default (package-private)
public
protected

questions.explanation: The `protected` modifier grants access to subclasses (even in different packages) and to all classes within the same package. There is no modifier that restricts same-package non-subclass access while allowing cross-package subclass access. However, `protected` is the closest — it allows subclass access across packages, which `default` (package-private) does not.

questions.prompt: What advantage does `ReentrantLock` offer over the `synchronized` keyword? ```java ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock(); lock.lock(); try { // critical section } finally { lock.unlock(); } ```

options.text: It is faster than synchronized in all scenarios
It supports tryLock(), interruptible locking, and fairness policies
It automatically releases the lock if an exception occurs
It allows locking across multiple JVM instances

questions.explanation: ReentrantLock provides features beyond synchronized: tryLock() for non-blocking lock attempts, lockInterruptibly() to respond to interrupts while waiting, fairness policies, and the ability to create multiple Condition objects. synchronized is simpler but less flexible.

questions.prompt: You override `equals()` in a class but forget to override `hashCode()`. What problem can this cause?

options.text: The JVM will automatically generate a matching hashCode()
The program will throw a CompilationError
Objects that are equal via equals() may not be found in a HashMap
equals() will stop working and always return false

questions.explanation: The contract between equals() and hashCode() states that equal objects must have the same hash code. If you override equals() without hashCode(), two logically equal objects may have different hash codes, causing them to be placed in different buckets in a HashMap/HashSet. This means lookups and deduplication will fail.

questions.prompt: What is the key difference between a slice and an array in Go? ```go arr := [3]int{1, 2, 3} slc := []int{1, 2, 3} ```

options.text: Arrays can grow dynamically, slices cannot
Arrays have a fixed size baked into their type; slices are dynamically-sized references to underlying arrays
Slices are stored on the stack, arrays on the heap
There is no difference — they are interchangeable

questions.explanation: Arrays in Go have a fixed size that is part of their type ([3]int is different from [4]int). Slices are dynamically-sized views backed by an underlying array. Slices have a length and capacity and can grow using append(). Arrays are value types and are copied on assignment.

questions.prompt: What does this code print? ```java Optional opt = Optional.of("Java"); String result = opt .filter(s -> s.length() > 10) .map(String::toUpperCase) .orElse("default"); System.out.println(result); ```

options.text: JAVA
Java
An empty string
default

questions.explanation: Optional.of("Java") creates an Optional containing "Java". The filter checks if length > 10 — "Java" has length 4, so the filter returns an empty Optional. The map is skipped on an empty Optional, and orElse returns "default".

questions.prompt: You are searching for a value in a sorted array of 1,000,000 elements using binary search. What is the maximum number of comparisons needed?
questions.explanation: Binary search halves the search space with each comparison. The maximum comparisons needed is ⌈log₂(1,000,000)⌉ = ⌈19.93⌉ = 20. This is why binary search is so efficient on sorted data.

questions.prompt: What does the `volatile` keyword guarantee in Java? ```java class Flag { private volatile boolean running = true; public void stop() { running = false; } public void run() { while (running) { /* work */ } } } ```

options.text: It makes all operations on the variable atomic
It prevents the variable from being garbage collected
It ensures changes to the variable are visible to all threads immediately
It locks the variable so only one thread can access it at a time

questions.explanation: The `volatile` keyword ensures that reads and writes to the variable go directly to main memory, providing visibility across threads. Without it, a thread might cache `running` in its CPU cache and never see the update from another thread. However, volatile does NOT make compound operations (like count++) atomic.

questions.prompt: What is the output of this code using `defer`? ```go func main() { fmt.Println("start") defer fmt.Println("deferred 1") defer fmt.Println("deferred 2") fmt.Println("end") } ```

options.text: start, end, deferred 1, deferred 2
start, deferred 1, deferred 2, end
start, end, deferred 2, deferred 1
deferred 1, deferred 2, start, end

questions.explanation: Deferred calls are executed in LIFO (last-in, first-out) order when the surrounding function returns. So 'start' and 'end' print first, then deferred calls execute in reverse order: 'deferred 2' then 'deferred 1'.

questions.prompt: What is the output of the following code? ```java String a = "hello"; String b = "hello"; String c = new String("hello"); System.out.println(a == b); System.out.println(a == c); ```

options.text: true, true
false, false
true, false
false, true

questions.explanation: String literals are interned in Java, so `a` and `b` refer to the same object in the string pool (a == b is true). Using `new String()` creates a new object on the heap, so `a == c` is false because == compares references, not content.

questions.prompt: What is the output of this Stream pipeline? ```java List words = List.of("hello", "world", "hi", "hey"); String result = words.stream() .filter(w -> w.startsWith("h")) .map(String::toUpperCase) .reduce("", (a, b) -> a + b + " "); System.out.println(result.trim()); ```

options.text: HELLO HI HEY
hello hi hey
HELLO WORLD HI HEY
HI HEY HELLO

questions.prompt: You have a DAG (directed acyclic graph) representing course prerequisites. You want to find a valid order to take all courses. Which algorithm produces this ordering?

options.text: Kruskal's algorithm
Dijkstra's algorithm
Floyd-Warshall algorithm
Topological sort

questions.explanation: Topological sort produces a linear ordering of vertices such that for every directed edge (u, v), u comes before v. This is exactly what's needed for course scheduling with prerequisites. It only works on DAGs — a cycle would mean circular prerequisites.

questions.prompt: What is the primary difference between memoization (top-down) and tabulation (bottom-up) in dynamic programming?

options.text: Memoization is always faster because it avoids unnecessary subproblems
Tabulation uses recursion while memoization uses iteration
Memoization solves subproblems recursively on demand; tabulation solves them iteratively from the bottom up
They are identical — the terms are interchangeable

questions.explanation: Memoization starts from the original problem and recurses down, caching results as they're computed — it only solves subproblems that are actually needed. Tabulation iteratively fills a table from the smallest subproblems up. Both avoid recomputation but differ in direction and control flow.

questions.prompt: Which `CompletableFuture` method should you use to transform a result asynchronously and return a new CompletableFuture? ```java CompletableFuture future = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> "hello"); // Goal: asynchronously convert to uppercase ```

options.text: thenApply(String::toUpperCase)
thenCompose(s -> s.toUpperCase())
thenAccept(s -> s.toUpperCase())
thenRun(() -> "HELLO")

questions.explanation: thenApply() transforms the result synchronously (like map), while thenCompose() is for chaining another CompletableFuture (like flatMap). thenAccept() consumes the result without returning a value. For a simple transformation, thenApply() is the correct choice — it takes a Function and returns a new CompletableFuture with the transformed value.

questions.prompt: In the activity selection problem, you have n activities with start and finish times. The greedy approach that always selects the activity with the earliest finish time is provably optimal. Why does selecting the shortest activity duration NOT work?

options.text: A short activity can block two or more non-overlapping activities that together would be a better choice
Short activities always overlap with more other activities
Duration-based selection is optimal but harder to implement
Shortest duration works for intervals but not for activities

questions.explanation: A short activity might overlap with two non-overlapping activities. For example, activities (0,4), (3,5), (4,8): the shortest is (3,5) with duration 2, but selecting it blocks both (0,4) and (4,8), giving 1 activity instead of the optimal 2. Earliest finish time avoids this by freeing up time for future activities.

questions.prompt: The Longest Common Subsequence (LCS) of 'ABCBDAB' and 'BDCAB' has what length?
questions.explanation: Building the LCS DP table for these strings, the longest common subsequence is 'BCAB' (length 4). The DP recurrence compares characters: if they match, extend the LCS; if not, take the max of skipping either character.

questions.prompt: A graph has 1,000 vertices and 5,000 edges. You need to store it and frequently check whether an edge exists between two specific vertices. Which representation is more space-efficient AND supports fast edge lookups?

options.text: Adjacency list with hash-set neighbors — O(V+E) space with O(1) expected edge lookup
Adjacency list with sorted neighbor arrays
Adjacency matrix — O(1) lookup justifies the space cost
Edge list sorted by source vertex

questions.explanation: An adjacency matrix provides O(1) edge lookup but uses O(V²) = O(1,000,000) space. An adjacency list uses O(V + E) = O(6,000) space but edge lookup is O(degree). A hash-set based adjacency list gives O(1) expected lookup with O(V + E) space — the best of both worlds for sparse graphs.

questions.prompt: A graph is bipartite if and only if it contains no odd-length cycles. Which algorithm can you use to test whether a graph is bipartite?

options.text: Topological sort — if it succeeds, the graph is bipartite
Find all cycles and check their lengths
Run Kruskal's and check if the MST has even weight
BFS with 2-coloring — assign alternating colors and check for conflicts

questions.explanation: BFS with 2-coloring attempts to assign alternating colors to adjacent nodes. If a conflict is found (two adjacent nodes with the same color), the graph is not bipartite. This runs in O(V + E) and is the standard bipartiteness test.

questions.prompt: When is linear search preferred over binary search, even when the data is sorted?

options.text: When the array has fewer than about 10 elements, where linear scan overhead is lower
When you need to find all occurrences of a value
When the data is stored on disk rather than in memory
Linear search is never preferred if the data is sorted

questions.explanation: For very small arrays (e.g., under 10 elements), linear search can be faster because it avoids the overhead of calculating midpoints and has better branch prediction. Binary search's O(log n) advantage only becomes meaningful at larger sizes.

questions.prompt: What is the effect of the `static` keyword on a method in Java? ```java class Counter { static int count = 0; static void increment() { count++; } } ```

options.text: The method can only be called from constructors
The method can access both instance and static fields directly
The method runs in a separate thread automatically
The method belongs to the class and can be called without an instance

questions.explanation: A static method belongs to the class rather than to any specific instance. It can be called without creating an object (Counter.increment()). Static methods can only directly access static fields and other static methods — they cannot use `this` or access instance members.

questions.prompt: You need to find the shortest path (fewest edges) from node A to node B in an unweighted graph. Which algorithm should you use?

options.text: Breadth-First Search (BFS)
Depth-First Search (DFS)
Bellman-Ford algorithm
Prim's algorithm

questions.explanation: BFS explores nodes level by level, guaranteeing that the first time it reaches any node, it has found the shortest path in terms of edge count. DFS may find a path but not necessarily the shortest one in an unweighted graph.

questions.prompt: Which of the following exceptions is a *checked* exception that must be caught or declared in a `throws` clause?

options.text: NullPointerException
ClassCastException
ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException
IOException

questions.explanation: IOException is a checked exception (extends Exception but not RuntimeException), so the compiler forces you to handle it. NullPointerException, ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException, and ClassCastException are all unchecked exceptions (they extend RuntimeException).

questions.prompt: You need to make change for 37 cents using coins of denominations [1, 5, 10, 25]. A greedy approach (always pick the largest coin that fits) gives 25+10+1+1 = 4 coins. Is greedy optimal here, and why?

options.text: No — greedy never works for coin change problems
Yes — greedy is always optimal for any coin denomination set
Yes — greedy works for US coins due to their denomination structure, but fails for arbitrary coin sets
No — DP gives 3 coins using 25+10+1+1

questions.explanation: For US coin denominations [1, 5, 10, 25], the greedy approach happens to always produce the optimal result. This is because these denominations have a special mathematical property where each denomination is at least twice the previous. However, this does NOT hold for arbitrary coin systems — e.g., with coins [1, 3, 4], greedy fails for amount 6.

questions.prompt: In quicksort, what happens if you always pick the first element as the pivot and the input array is already sorted in ascending order?

options.text: It runs in O(n log n) since the array is already sorted
It runs in O(n) since no swaps are needed
It runs in O(n log n) but uses extra memory
It degrades to O(n²) because every partition is maximally unbalanced

questions.explanation: When the first element is always the pivot on a sorted array, every partition produces one empty subarray and one subarray of size n−1. This creates n levels of recursion with O(n) work each, resulting in O(n²) total time — quicksort's worst case.

questions.prompt: What does this code print? ```java Integer x = 127; Integer y = 127; Integer a = 128; Integer b = 128; System.out.println(x == y); System.out.println(a == b); ```

options.text: true, false
true, true
false, false
false, true

questions.explanation: Java caches Integer values between -128 and 127 (autoboxing cache). So x and y reference the same cached object (x == y is true). Values outside this range like 128 create new objects, so a == b is false because they are different references.

questions.prompt: What happens when you send a value on an unbuffered channel with no receiver ready? ```go ch := make(chan int) ch <- 42 // What happens here? ```

options.text: The value 42 is silently discarded
A compile-time error is raised
The value is buffered automatically until a receiver is ready
The goroutine blocks forever, causing a deadlock

If you send on an unbuffered channel from the main goroutine with no goroutine ready to receive, the program deadlocks. The Go runtime detects this and panics with 'fatal error: all goroutines are asleep - deadlock!'.

questions.prompt: In the 0/1 knapsack problem with n items and capacity W, what is the time and space complexity of the standard DP solution?

options.text: Time O(n × W), Space O(n × W)
Time O(2^n), Space O(n)
Time O(n log W), Space O(n)
Time O(n²), Space O(n²)

questions.explanation: The standard 0/1 knapsack DP uses a 2D table of size n × W, filling each cell in O(1) time. This gives O(n × W) time and space. Note this is pseudo-polynomial — it's polynomial in the numeric value of W, not in the number of bits needed to represent W.

questions.prompt: You compute Fibonacci(50) using naive recursion. Approximately how many function calls are made versus using memoization?

options.text: About 50 calls for both — recursion depth is the same
About 2,500 naive vs 50 memoized
About 10^6 naive vs 100 memoized
About 10^15 naive vs 51 memoized

questions.explanation: Naive recursive Fibonacci has exponential time complexity O(2^n), resulting in roughly 2^50 ≈ 10^15 calls for Fib(50). With memoization, each value from Fib(0) to Fib(50) is computed exactly once, giving just 51 unique computations with O(n) total calls.

questions.prompt: What does this sealed class hierarchy permit? ```java public sealed class Shape permits Circle, Rectangle {} public final class Circle extends Shape { } public non-sealed class Rectangle extends Shape { } ```

options.text: Any class in the same module can extend Shape freely
Only Circle and Rectangle can extend Shape; Circle cannot be extended, but Rectangle can be
Neither Circle nor Rectangle can be extended further
The sealed keyword is only for documentation and has no compile-time effect

questions.explanation: Sealed classes restrict which classes can extend them — only those listed in the `permits` clause. Circle is `final` so it cannot be further extended. Rectangle is `non-sealed`, meaning any class can extend Rectangle. questions.prompt: You are building a network of cables to connect 8 offices with minimum total cable length. You have a weighted graph of all possible connections. Both Prim's and Kruskal's algorithms can solve this. When would Kruskal's likely outperform Prim's?

options.text: When the graph is dense (many edges between offices)
When the graph is sparse (offices have few possible connections)
When all edge weights are equal
When the graph contains negative weights

questions.explanation: Kruskal's sorts all edges and processes them with Union-Find, running in O(E log E). It's efficient when E is small relative to V² (sparse graphs). Prim's with an adjacency matrix runs in O(V²), which is better for dense graphs where E ≈ V².

questions.prompt: The edit distance (Levenshtein distance) between 'kitten' and 'sitting' is computed using DP. What operations does it consider, and what is the result?

options.text: Insert and delete only; distance is 4

Insert, delete, and substitute; distance is 3

For 'kitten' → 'sitting': substitute k→s, substitute e→i, insert g at the end = 3 operations. The DP table is filled using the recurrence that takes the minimum of these three choices at each position.

questions.prompt: Where are local variables stored in the JVM memory model?

options.text: In the thread's stack frame
In the metaspace (formerly PermGen)
In the heap alongside object instances
In the string pool area

questions.explanation: Each thread has its own stack, and local variables (including method parameters and primitive values) are stored in stack frames on that thread's stack. Objects themselves are on the heap, but the reference variable pointing to them is on the stack.

questions.prompt: Which functional interface should you use for a lambda that takes a `String` and returns an `Integer`?

options.text: Consumer
Supplier
Function
Predicate

questions.explanation: Function represents a function that takes an argument of type T and returns a result of type R. Function takes a String and returns an Integer. Consumer takes input but returns nothing, Supplier takes nothing and returns a value, and Predicate takes input and returns a boolean.

questions.prompt: What is the time complexity of the Bellman-Ford algorithm for a graph with V vertices and E edges?

options.text: O(V log V)
O(E log V)
O(V × E)
O(V²)

questions.explanation: Bellman-Ford relaxes all E edges in each of V−1 iterations (since the longest shortest path can have at most V−1 edges). This gives O(V × E) time complexity. It's slower than Dijkstra but handles negative weights correctly.

questions.prompt: The A* search algorithm uses a heuristic function h(n) to guide its search. For A* to guarantee finding the optimal path, what property must h(n) satisfy?

options.text: h(n) must be consistent but can overestimate
h(n) must equal the exact cost to the goal
h(n) must be admissible — it never overestimates the true cost to the goal
h(n) must always return zero for correctness

questions.explanation: A* requires an admissible heuristic — one that never overestimates the true cost to the goal. This ensures A* won't skip the optimal path. If h(n) overestimates, A* might prune the optimal path too early, finding a suboptimal solution instead.

questions.prompt: What does this pattern matching code (Java 17+) print? ```java Object obj = "Hello World"; if (obj instanceof String s && s.length() > 5) { System.out.println(s.toUpperCase()); } else { System.out.println("short"); } ```

short
A ClassCastException is thrown
HELLO WORLD

questions.prompt: Consider the following Java code: ```java interface Flyable { void fly(); } abstract class Bird { abstract void sing(); } class Sparrow extends Bird implements Flyable { void sing() { System.out.println("Tweet"); } public void fly() { System.out.println("Flap"); } } ``` Which statement about this code is correct?

It compiles because a class can extend one class and implement multiple interfaces

It won't compile because sing() needs the public modifier in Sparrow

questions.prompt: Given the following code, what is the value of `list` after execution? ```java List list = new ArrayList(Arrays.asList("a", "b", "c")); list.set(1, "x"); list.add(1, "y"); ```

questions.prompt: What are the two key properties a problem must exhibit for dynamic programming to be applicable?

options.text: Overlapping subproblems and optimal substructure
Greedy choice property and optimal substructure
Divide-and-conquer structure and polynomial time
Memoization capability and constant space usage

questions.explanation: Dynamic programming requires (1) overlapping subproblems — the same smaller problems are solved repeatedly, and (2) optimal substructure — an optimal solution can be constructed from optimal solutions of its subproblems. Without both, DP provides no advantage over other techniques.

questions.prompt: You need to sort 10 million integers that range from 0 to 999. Which approach would be most efficient?

options.text: Quicksort with random pivot — it's always the fastest general sort
Counting sort — the small value range (0–999) makes it O(n)
Merge sort — guaranteed O(n log n) is best for large inputs
